title: Bengal's Chingri Malai Curry Ranks Among the World's Best Shrimp Dishes on TasteAtlas, the Only Indian Entry in the Top 50
excerpt: The coconut-milk prawn curry, a Bengali wedding and festival staple, has earned 11th place in TasteAtlas' global ranking of best shrimp dishes — beating out entries from Japan, Thailand, and Indonesia.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Chingri Malai Curry ranks 11th in TasteAtlas' best shrimp dishes, the only Indian entry in the top 50.
  • Mexico's Tacos Gobernador and Spain's Gambas al Ajillo top the global ranking, featuring dishes from 20 countries.
  • The dish's origins trace back to trade with Malaysian merchants, evolving into a distinct Bengali identity.
  • Chingri Malai Curry is a staple at Bengali weddings and celebrations, symbolizing cultural identity.

  • The dish is a staple at Bengali weddings, Pohela Boishakh celebrations, and family gatherings across India and the diaspora

India's Sole Entry in a Crowded Field

Bengal's iconic Chingri Malai Curry has earned a place among the world's finest shrimp dishes in TasteAtlas' latest global ranking, landing at 11th and standing as the only Indian dish in the prestigious top 50.

The list, which spans preparations from more than 20 countries, is dominated by Latin American and Mediterranean cuisines. Mexico's Tacos Gobernador and Camarones al Mojo de Ajo took the top two spots, followed by Spain's Gambas al Ajillo, Gambas a la Plancha, and Brazil's Bobó de Camarão. Entries from Greece, Peru, and China round out the top ten.

Chingri Malai Curry's 11th-place finish beat out shrimp and prawn preparations from Japan, Thailand, Indonesia, and several European nations — a notable achievement for a regional Indian dish competing against globally exported cuisines with far larger marketing footprints.

What Makes the Dish Special

Also known as Malai Chingri or Prawn Malai Curry, the dish features fresh prawns — ideally large freshwater golda chingri — simmered in a luxurious gravy built on a base of coconut milk. The sauce gets its warmth from garam masala, turmeric, green chillies, ginger, and garlic, with whole spices including cardamom, cinnamon, and cloves adding layers of aroma. A finish of ghee or mustard oil with finely sliced onions brings the signature balance of sweet, spicy, and creamy that lets the natural sweetness of the prawns shine through.

Cultural Significance of Chingri Malai Curry
›A staple at Bengali weddings and celebrations.
›Represents cultural identity for the Bengali diaspora.
›Served alongside steaming white rice.
›Connects communities across continents.

Chef and food writer Sadaf Hussain, speaking to The Indian Express, called Chingri Malai Curry a "classic" while noting its complex culinary lineage. "Malaysian and Singaporean cuisines typically use ingredients such as lemongrass and galangal, whereas Bengali versions do not," he said, pointing to how the dish has evolved into something with its own distinct identity.

"Chingri Malai Curry is a classic. While it may share some influence with Malay or Malaysian culinary traditions, it has evolved into a distinct dish with its own identity."

— Sadaf Hussain, Chef and Food Writer

A Dish Rooted in Trade and Celebration

Food historians trace the dish's name to Bengal's historical trade with Malaysian merchants. The word "malai" is believed to derive from "Malay," pointing to the coconut milk that forms the curry's backbone — an ingredient that arrived in Bengali kitchens through centuries of maritime commerce. TasteAtlas notes this connection on the dish's official page, describing it as a curry that "made its way to Bengali kitchens through contact with Malaysian traders."

Today, Chingri Malai Curry is a fixture of Bengali celebrations. From weddings to Pohela Boishakh, the Bengali New Year, to intimate family gatherings, it occupies a central place on the table. Typically served alongside steaming white rice, the dish is as much a marker of cultural identity as it is a culinary achievement.

For the Bengali diaspora, the recognition carries particular resonance. Chingri Malai Curry is one of the dishes that travel well — replicated in kitchens from New Jersey to London to Singapore, a taste of home that connects communities across continents. Its place on a global ranking confirms what Bengali food lovers have always known: this is world-class cuisine that has simply been waiting for the world to catch up.
